   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a proposal you made with start_session (initiation "own_initiative" or "offer") that the user has not started.

Call this when it went stale: the work was done here after all (by you or the user), it turned out unnecessary, or you proposed a better-scoped replacement (propose the new one first, then dismiss the old task_id). A card the user answered has already left, "Do it here" included, so it needs no call.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__hand_off_to_session
tools.description: Move the task you are in the middle of into its own session (a fork of this conversation plus your remaining plan) so you can answer the user now. Use it when a new user message about something else arrives mid-task — not for small corrections or when the user said to keep the work here. In a worktree the fork gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip: commit first (uncommitted edits stay here). Bold title line and one sentence right before the call; after it, stop that task here and answer the new message — no recap.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

content.content:
209:To reduce upload traffic, the cohort size $m_t=|C_k^t|$ is adjusted dynamically from the convergence efficiency $\rho^{t-1}$ of the previous round (Eq.~(16)) and is bounded by $C_{k_{\min}} \le m_t \le C_{k_{\max}}$, where $C_{k_{\min}}$ and $C_{k_{\max}}$ are the lower and upper bounds, respectively.
324:5.  & \hspace{2em}Compute the cohort size $m_t$ using (16) from $\rho^{t-1}$\\
412:The deviation control signal $\nu^t$ is computed on the server from completed rounds only. It is the difference between a reference convergence rate $\Omega^t$ and the relative validation-loss reduction $\rho^{t-1}$ of the previous round (Eq.~(15)), as shown in Eq.~(10), and it is the feedback input of Eq.~(8). A positive $\nu^t$ means that the previous round converged more slowly than the reference; a non-positive value means that it converged at least as fast.
414:\nu^t = \Omega^t - \rho^{t-1}\qquad (t \ge 2)
454:On the server-side, it receives fitness scores from all clients for evaluation. The server ranks the clients according to their fitness scores and adaptively determines the cohort size $m_t=|C_k^t|$ according to the convergence efficiency observed in the previous communication round, namely the relative reduction $\rho^{t-1}$ of the validation loss as shown in Eq. (15). Two predefined integer bounds, $C_{k_{\min}}$ and $C_{k_{\max}}$ (fixed in advance for each configuration), regulate the allowable cohort size range (McMahan et al. 2017; Li et al. 2020), thereby enabling an adaptive number of clients to be selected for aggregation while maintaining communication efficiency and mitigating network congestion, as defined in Eq. (16). Here $L_{global}^{t}$ is the validation loss after round $t$ and $L_{global}^{0}$ that of the initial model. Hence $\rho^{t}\le 1$: it is positive when the loss falls and negative when it rises, and a negative value is kept because it selects the maximum cohort. If the previous loss is zero or non-finite, $\rho^{t}$ is undefined and the round is cancelled with all state unchanged.
455:% REVISED (Replacement 3): Eq. (15) written for the completed round t (selection in round t uses rho^{t-1})
463:m_t = \min\left\{C_{k_{\max}},\ \max\left\{C_{k_{\min}},\ \left\lfloor C_{k_{\min}} + (C_{k_{\max}} - C_{k_{\min}})\big[1-\mathrm{clip}(\rho^{t-1},0,1)\big] + \tfrac{1}{2}\right\rfloor\right\}\right\}
467:A large $\rho^{t-1}$ means fast progress, so a smaller cohort suffices and the uploads fall; stagnation or a loss increase ($\rho^{t-1}\le 0$) and the first round select $C_{k_{\max}}$, since averaging more clients reduces the variance of the aggregate. Values in between are interpolated linearly and rounded to the nearest integer. Since $\rho^{t-1}$ alone keeps the cohort near $C_{k_{\max}}$, the ratio $\rho^{t-1}/\Omega^{t}$ can replace it, which spans the full range and lowers the uploads without a detectable change in accuracy (Table~\ref{tab:cohort}). Clients with a non-finite update are excluded; if fewer than $m_t$ remain, all are selected.
1285:\textbf{Cohort size.} Eq.~(16) with the absolute loss reduction $\rho^{t-1}$ keeps the cohort at $C_{k_{\max}}$ in 75\% of the rounds and never below 7 clients in the 45 runs of the reproduction study (mean 9.71 [9.68, 9.75] clients, i.e.\ 2.9\% fewer uploads than a fixed cohort of ten). Measuring the efficiency against the reference pace of the run (the ratio $\rho^{t-1}/\Omega^{t}$ in place of $\rho^{t-1}$ in Eq.~(16)) uses the whole range from 5 to 10 clients: in Table~\ref{tab:cohort} the mean cohort falls from 9.83 to 9.10 clients and the upload volume by 7.5\% relative to the absolute rule (9.0\% relative to a fixed cohort), with best-round accuracy $-0.29$ [$-0.57$, $+0.05$] and last-10-round accuracy $-0.08$ [$-0.55$, $+0.41$] points, Jain index 0.997 against 0.998 and no unselected client; the longest wait rises from 10.8 to 14.0 rounds, below the threshold $R=20$ of the waiting-time guard. The saving of either rule is bounded by $1-C_{k_{\min}}/C_{k_{\max}}$. The cohort size is the number of uploads per round; the cumulative uploads to a target accuracy are the sum of the cohort sizes over the rounds needed to reach it, so that a reduction of the cumulative count can come from smaller cohorts or from fewer rounds, and the two are reported separately (Section~\ref{sec:score_analysis} and the round-to-target columns of Section 5).

content: ما هو cohort؟

content.text:
الـ **cohort** هو مجموعة العملاء (clients) التي يختارها السيرفر في جولة معينة ليرفعوا تحديثاتهم (uploads) ويدخلوا في تجميع النموذج العام (aggregation).

**مثال:** في FedFACS يوجد N = 100 عميل مرشح. كلهم يحمّلون النموذج ويتدرّبون محلياً ويحسبون الـ fitness score. بعدها يختار السيرفر الأعلى score فقط، مثلاً 7 عملاء. هؤلاء السبعة هم الـ cohort في هذه الجولة، وهم وحدهم من يرفع التحديث.

**حجم الـ cohort** (الرمز m_t) يتغير من جولة لأخرى. يقع دائماً بين حدّين: الأدنى Cmin = 5 والأعلى Cmax = 10 في التجارب المعاد إنتاجها.
- إذا كان التدريب يتحسن بسرعة، يصغر الـ cohort فيقل حجم الرفع.
- إذا توقف التحسن أو زادت الـ loss، يكبر الـ cohort حتى Cmax. التجميع على عدد أكبر من العملاء يقلل التباين في النموذج المجمّع.

كلمة cohort نفسها مستخدمة في الورقة الأصلية، وهي مرادفة هنا لـ "الـ clients المشاركين في الجولة" (participating clients). إن أردت، أضيف في الورقة جملة تعريف قصيرة عند أول ذكر لها.

The experimental setup follows configuration A, and The target accuracy is determined as the maximum accuracy obtained by FedAvg under the corresponding experiments with data partitioning conditions presented in scenarios 1 and 2.

Moreover, dynamic cohort sizing (FedFACS-A2) changes the accuracy only slightly. Relative to a fixed cohort of $C_{k_{\max}}$ clients, it saves the fraction by which the mean cohort size falls below $C_{k_{\max}}$; this fraction cannot exceed $1-C_{k_{\min}}/C_{k_{\max}}$, so it grows with the distance between the two bounds (Table~\ref{tab:cohort}). content.text:
**FedFACS-A2** هو نسخة الـ ablation الثانية، وتُستخدم لقياس أثر مكوّن واحد: **تغيير حجم الـ cohort ديناميكياً**.

الإصدارات الثلاثة في دراسة الـ ablation (القسم 5.1، Configuration A):

| النسخة | اختيار العملاء حسب الـ fitness | حجم الـ cohort | التجميع (aggregation) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FedFACS-A1** | نعم | ثابت (10) | بحسب عدد العينات (static، مثل FedAvg) |
| **FedFACS-A2** | نعم | **ديناميكي** (بين Cmin و Cmax) | بحسب عدد العينات |
| **FedFACS** (الكامل) | نعم | ديناميكي | أوزان الاستقرار (stability weights) في Eq. 18 |

بالمقارنة بين النسخ:
- A1 مقابل A2 يبيّن أثر **حجم الـ cohort الديناميكي** وحده.
- A2 مقابل الكامل يبيّن أثر **أوزان الاستقرار** وحدها.

ولهذا تتحدث الجملة التي عدّلناها في 5.1 عن A2: هي الحلقة التي تقيس توفير الرفع (upload) الناتج عن الـ cohort الديناميكي.

**ملاحظة:** نص الورقة الحالي (سطر 604) يذكر Cmin = 8 في A2، بينما التجارب المعاد إنتاجها استخدمت 5 و10. تحتاج هذه الأرقام تأكيداً من المؤلفين: هل الإعداد الأصلي 8–10 أم 5–10؟ أصلحها حسب إجابتهم.

content.content:
99:Federated Learning (FL) is a distributed learning framework that enables clients to jointly optimize a common model through server coordination, while their local training data remain within their respective environments. Despite its privacy advantages, FL encounters significant challenges resulting from the participation of numerous clients having heterogeneous data during each training round. Consequently, this degrades accuracy, delays convergence, increases the communication overhead, and undermines fairness among participating clients. Hence, Client Selection (CS) has become essential for identifying the most beneficial clients for global model training. However, existing approaches often struggle to preserve model accuracy and fairness while limiting communication costs in the presence of non-Independent and Identically Distributed (non-IID) data. In response to these challenges, we introduce FedFACS (Federated Fair Adaptive Client Selection), a novel framework designed to handle data heterogeneity while improving fairness and training efficiency. FedFACS formulates client selection using a multi-objective fitness function combining the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between local and global predictions with a dynamic fairness baseline. In addition, we incorporate an uncertainty-aware penalty that mitigates the impact of local noise. Moreover, a control mechanism is introduced to adaptively balance utility and fairness in response to global convergence feedback. A dynamic cohort sizing mechanism was developed that identifies the optimal number of high-fitness clients needed for each round. Furthermore, we propose a nonnegative normalised aggregation family whose default, the sample-count weighting, keeps the aggregate consistent with the population objective, and we compare it with stability weighting. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets under several data heterogeneous settings show that FedFACS achieves average improvements of 1.39\% in accuracy, 1.41\% in F1-score, and 0.44\% in recall, as well as 3.47\% fewer selected clients while maintaining comparable communication rounds, in addition to improving fairness by an average of 1.38\% in Jain's Fairness Index (JFI), relative to the best performing existing method, thereby enhancing performance and reducing communication overhead while ensuring fairness.
156:\subsection{Classical Federated Learning}
162:\subsection{Modern Client Selection and Model Aggregation}
172:\subsection{Fairness-Based Client Selection}
223:\subsection{FedFACS Overview}
349:\subsection{FedFACS Methodology}
403:The fairness term grows while a client remains unselected, so that long-waiting clients rise in the priority of Eq. (9), where $\Pi_i^t$ is the priority score of client $i$ at round $t$ and $a_i^t$ weights utility against fairness. Since $F_i^t \ge 1$ and the feedback rule keeps the mixing coefficient small, the priority is determined mainly by the fairness term: the utility term orders the clients with similar waiting times, so that no client is excluded by a low utility. Section~\ref{sec:score_analysis} shows that this is the regime in which FedFACS reaches its highest accuracy at near-uniform participation: weighting the two terms comparably, either with a constant coefficient of 0.5 or by rank normalisation, lowers the Jain index and does not raise accuracy, and no constant coefficient tested is significantly more accurate than the feedback rule, which sets the coefficient without tuning.
498:\subsection{Properties of FedFACS}\label{sec:properties}
521:\subsection{Datasets}
527:\subsection{Model and experimental setup}
543:\textbf{Performance metrics}. The proposed framework is examined with respect to performance, fairness, and communication efficiency using the following evaluation metrics:
586:\textit{Jain's Fairness Index (JFI)}: quantifies the fairness of participation on the quality-adjusted participation $p_i/q_i$ (Shi et al. 2024; Cho et al. 2020).
600:\subsection{Experimental Results and Analysis}
1180:\caption{Jain Fairness Index (JFI) comparison under Scenarios 3 and 4 for CIFAR-10 and FMNIST. Darker colors denote higher fairness values.}
1212:\subsection{Analysis of the selection score}\label{sec:score_analysis}
1255:\textbf{Fairness term and mixing coefficient.} At the diagnostic rounds 5 to 100 the fairness term has a median of 1.88 and the utility score $\Delta KL_i^t$ a median of 0.73, and the coefficients have a median of 0.10 (below). The weighted utility term $a_i^t\Delta KL_i^t$ is therefore a median 3\% of $(1-a_i^t)F_i^t$, the priority of Eq.~(9) is rank-correlated with $F_i^t$ (Spearman 0.92 against 0.27 for $\Delta KL_i^t$), and 98.9\% of the selected clients have a fairness term above the median: the priority is determined mainly by the waiting time, and the utility term orders the clients with similar waiting times. Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows that this regime is the one that works. Without the fairness term ($a=1$) the Jain index falls to 0.56 and 0.35, 10.0\% and 20.3\% of the clients are never selected, and accuracy decreases by 2.6 and 2.2 points. A balanced constant $a=0.5$ lowers the Jain index to 0.92 and 0.94, lengthens the longest wait to 14--16 rounds, and lowers accuracy (best round, CIFAR-10: $-1.25$ [$-1.90$, $-0.73$]; last 10 rounds, FMNIST: $-1.53$ [$-3.42$, $-0.29$]). Rank-normalising both terms so that they carry equal weight, together with the waiting-time guard and with $a\in\{0.25,0.5\}$, gave the same outcome: the Jain index fell to 0.94--0.99, the longest wait rose to 17--20 rounds, and accuracy did not improve ($-0.5$ to $-0.8$ points). At the diagnostic rounds 5 to 100 the coefficients of the clients have a median of 0.10 (mean 0.14; 5th--95th percentile 0.001--0.33). In accuracy, no constant is significantly better than the feedback rule in any comparison, and the rule is significantly better in some ($a=0.05$ on CIFAR-10, best round: $-0.80$ [$-1.91$, $-0.10$] for the constant; $a=0.10$ on FMNIST, last 10 rounds: $-0.90$ [$-1.33$, $-0.30$]); the constants $a=0.05$ and $a=0.10$ differ from it by at most one round in the longest wait and by at most 0.002 in the Jain index. The rule thus provides this operating point without requiring the coefficient to be tuned.

99:Federated Learning (FL) is a distributed learning framework that enables clients to jointly optimize a common model through server coordination, while their local training data remain within their respective environments. Despite its privacy advantages, FL encounters significant challenges resulting from the participation of numerous clients having heterogeneous data during each training round. Consequently, this degrades accuracy, delays convergence, increases the communication overhead, and undermines fairness among participating clients. Hence, Client Selection (CS) has become essential for identifying the most beneficial clients for global model training. However, existing approaches often struggle to preserve model accuracy and fairness while limiting communication costs in the presence of non-Independent and Identically Distributed (non-IID) data. In response to these challenges, we introduce FedFACS (Federated Fair Adaptive Client Selection), a novel framework designed to handle data heterogeneity while improving fairness and training efficiency. FedFACS formulates client selection using a multi-objective fitness function combining the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between local and global predictions with a dynamic fairness baseline. In addition, we incorporate an uncertainty-aware penalty that mitigates the impact of local noise. Moreover, a control mechanism is introduced to adaptively balance utility and fairness in response to global convergence feedback. A dynamic cohort sizing mechanism was developed that identifies the optimal number of high-fitness clients needed for each round. Furthermore, we propose a nonnegative normalised aggregation family whose default, the sample-count weighting, keeps the aggregate consistent with the population objective, and we compare it with stability weighting. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets under several data heterogeneous settings show that FedFACS achieves average improvements of 1.39\% in accuracy, 1.41\% in F1-score, and 0.44\% in recall, as well as 3.47\% fewer selected clients while maintaining comparable communication rounds, in addition to improving fairness by an average of 1.38\% in Jain's Fairness Index (JFI), relative to the best performing existing method, thereby enhancing performance and reducing communication overhead while ensuring fairness.

2 My first concern is that the stated fairness mechanism does not implement the behavior described in the manuscript. Equation (7) resets the idle-round counter to zero when a client is selected but leaves it unchanged when the client is not selected. Consequently, with zero initialization, every counter remains zero throughout training, and Equation (6) gives the same fairness value of one for every client. This contradicts the repeated explanation that fairness priority increases as a client remains unselected. Please establish whether the implementation increments the counter for an unselected client and whether Equation (7) is a transcription error. The counter initialization, update timing, and calculation of the population average must be specified consistently. This distinction is essential because the reported fairness improvements cannot presently be attributed to the mechanism as written.

9 The principal communication-efficiency claim is not established by the reported participation counts. According to the architecture and Algorithms 1 and 2, all candidate clients receive the global model, perform local training, calculate scores, and report those scores before the server selects the clients whose model updates will be uploaded and aggregated. Thus, the proposed mechanism selects uploads and aggregation contributions after local training; it does not necessarily reduce the number of clients that download the model or perform computation. Counting only aggregated client updates excludes potentially substantial downlink, scoring, and discarded-training costs. Please distinguish candidate clients, locally trained clients, uploading clients, and aggregated clients, and report total transmitted bytes, local computation, scoring overhead, and elapsed time under an explicit communication model. Fewer uploaded updates can be a useful result, but it is not sufficient evidence of lower overall communication or training cost.

10 The fairness metric is interpreted incorrectly. Equation (24) applies Jain�s index to the quality-adjusted quantities \(p_i/q_i\). Therefore, an index of one corresponds to equal participation relative to quality, meaning \(p_i\) is proportional to \(q_i\); it does not generally correspond to equal raw participation. This also undermines the later argument that avoiding an index of one avoids forced uniform participation. Furthermore, an index between 0.5 and one does not establish that every client participates. For example, with equal client quality, uniformly serving 90 of 100 clients while never serving the remaining ten gives an index of 0.9. Please define the intended fairness objective consistently and distinguish participation equality, quality-proportional participation, and fairness of predictive outcomes. The proposed interpretation of 0.5 as a fairness boundary also requires justification.

22 Finally, the algorithms should be rewritten to provide one consistent, executable account of the method. The client procedure should explicitly state whether local parameters are reset to the received global parameters at every round, when scoring predictions are computed, and when counters are updated. The server procedure should identify all received information and use the same aggregation formula as the mathematical section. A reproducibility package containing configuration files, partition identifiers, seeds, per-round scores, cohort selections, aggregation weights, and metric outputs would make the central claims auditable. Privacy statements should be restricted to the demonstrated property that raw training data remain local unless an additional privacy analysis is supplied. Claims of scalability and practical deployment should likewise be limited to the synchronous simulated setting unless supported by measurements under increasing client populations and realistic participation constraints.

30 1. Hidden communication and computation cost. According to Algorithms 1�2, the server broadcasts the model to all clients, and all clients train for E epochs and compute KL and fitness. Only the upload is reduced. Baselines such as FedAvg train only the sampled clients, and Pow-D's probing cost is not counted. Downlink and local-compute costs must be reported; otherwise the �communication-efficient� claim is misleading and the comparison is unfair.

32 3. Incorrect update rule (Eq. 7). An unselected client's idle counter stays at r_i^t and never increases. This contradicts the text, under which fairness grows as a client waits. The fairness mechanism as written cannot work.

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
RES, OUT = os.path.join(HERE, "results"), os.path.join(HERE, "analysis")
os.makedirs(OUT, exist_ok=True)
MAIN_METHODS = ["random", "fedprox", "fednova", "qffl", "powd", "oort", "divfl", "fedfacs"]
ABL = ["fedfacs", "abl_A1", "abl_A2", "abl_fixmix", "abl_nofair", "abl_nopen", "abl_loss", "abl_randscore", "abl_rescale"]


def jain(x):
    x = np.asarray(x, float)
    return float(x.sum() ** 2 / (len(x) * (x ** 2).sum())) if (x ** 2).sum() > 0 else 0.0


def load():
    rows = []
    for p in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(RES, "*.json"))):
        r = json.load(open(p))
        c = r["cfg"]
        tag = re.sub(r"^.*_s\d+", "", os.path.basename(p)[:-5])
        rows.append((c["dataset"], c["scenario"], c["method"], c["seed"], tag, r))
    return rows


def run_metrics(r, target=None):
    lg = r["log"]
    va, ta = np.array(lg["val_acc"]), np.array(lg["test_acc"])
    sc = np.array(r["sel_count"], float)
    noise = np.array(r.get("noise", np.zeros(len(sc))))
    q = 10.0 * (1.0 - noise)
    pc = np.array(r["per_client_acc"])
    cm = np.array(r["confusion"], float)
    tp = np.diag(cm)
    rec = tp / np.maximum(cm.sum(1), 1)
    prec = tp / np.maximum(cm.sum(0), 1)
    f1 = 2 * prec * rec / np.maximum(prec + rec, 1e-12)
    m = dict(acc_best=ta[int(va.argmax())] * 100, acc_last10=ta[-10:].mean() * 100, acc_final=ta[-1] * 100,
             val_best=va.max() * 100, macro_recall=rec.mean() * 100, macro_prec=prec.mean() * 100, macro_f1=f1.mean() * 100,
             acc_from_cm=tp.sum() / cm.sum() * 100,
             jfi=jain(sc), jfi_q=jain(sc / q), never=(sc == 0).mean() * 100, max_wait=max(r["max_wait"]),
             pc_mean=pc.mean() * 100, pc_std=pc.std() * 100, pc_p10=np.percentile(pc, 10) * 100,
             cohort=np.mean(lg["cohort"]), up_gb=lg["up"][-1] / 1e9, down_gb=lg["down"][-1] / 1e9,
             steps_m=lg["steps"][-1] / 1e6, wall=np.mean(lg["wall"]), peak_mb=r.get("peak_mem_mb", np.nan),
             clip=r.get("clip_hits", 0), failed=r.get("failed_updates", 0), invalid=r.get("invalid_rounds", 0),
             jitter=np.abs(np.diff(ta[-30:])).mean() * 100)
    if target is not None:
        hit = np.where(va >= target)[0]
        rr = int(hit[0]) + 1 if len(hit) else None
        m["r2t"] = rr
        for k in ("up", "down"):
            m[k + "_gb_r2t"] = lg[k][rr - 1] / 1e9 if rr else None
        m["steps_m_r2t"] = lg["steps"][rr - 1] / 1e6 if rr else None
    return m


def ms(x, fmt="{:.2f}"):
    x = np.array([v for v in x if v is not None and not (isinstance(v, float) and np.isnan(v))], float)
    if len(x) == 0:
        return "n/a"
    return fmt.format(x.mean()) + (" ± " + fmt.format(x.std(ddof=1)) if len(x) > 1 else "")

"""Builds FedFACS_Replacements_7_8.docx (cohort size; aggregation weights): Before/After with locations, declarations, evidence."""
import os
import subprocess
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
import docx
import pypandoc
from docx.enum.text import WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH
from docx.shared import Inches, Pt

import build_final56 as B

P, WORK, BS = B.P, B.WORK, B.BS
OUTF = os.path.join(P, "FedFACS_Replacements_7_8.docx")
ORIG, REV = B.ORIG, B.REV


def to_eol(text, start):
    i = text.index(start)
    j = text.find("\n", i)
    return text[i:j if j >= 0 else len(text)]


def seg(text, start, end):
    i = text.index(start)
    j = text.index(end, i) + len(end)
    return text[i:j]


def upto_eol(text, start, last):
    i = text.index(start)
    k = text.index(last, i)
    j = text.find(chr(10), k)
    return text[i:j if j >= 0 else len(text)]


EQ = lambda lab: BS + "label{" + lab + "}\n" + BS + "end{equation}"
HEAD = r"""
::: {custom-style="BA-Title"}
FedFACS: Replacements 7 and 8 (cohort size; aggregation weights)
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Note"}
Scope. Replacement 7 covers the cohort-size rule (Eqs. (15)-(16)), its bounds and the claim on fewer clients per round; Replacement 8 covers the aggregation weights (Eqs. (4), (17)-(18)), their relation to the objective of Eq. (1) and the reporting of participation and influence. Locations refer to the original sn-article.tex. Evidence comes from our reproduced runs (ResNet-18 with frozen early layers, 100 clients, 100 rounds, cohorts of 5 to 10 clients; 95% bootstrap intervals); the manuscript must state that its numbers come from this implementation. Colours: [red]{custom-style="Del"} = removed, [green]{custom-style="Add"} = added.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Note"}
NEW ELEMENTS. The original paper has no Section 4.3, no Section 5.4, no Tables Y, Z, W and no Eq. (18) with the coefficient kappa. They are new: the full text of Section 4.3 is in part 3a of this file (insert it after Section 4.2); the new paragraphs of Section 5.4 and Tables Z and W are in part 3 (Section 5.4 is inserted at the end of Section 5, before the Conclusion; its remaining paragraphs and Tables X, X2, Y are in the Replacement 5 file).
:::

# 1. What each comment receives: fix, location, evidence, declaration
"""

COMMENTS = [
    ("Replacement 7. R1-06 and R2-08: validity, indexing and rounding of the cohort rule",
     "Eq. (15) is written for the completed round and Eq. (16) uses the previous round, so that no future loss is needed. The efficiency is clipped to [0,1], the cohort is an integer obtained by half-up rounding and clamped to [Cmin, Cmax], the history starts at rho^0 = 0 (the first rounds select Cmax), a zero or non-finite previous loss cancels the round, and a candidate whose update is not finite is unavailable. The rule is nonincreasing in the efficiency, and any two rounding conventions differ by at most one client.",
     "Section 4.2, Eqs. (15)-(16) and the paragraph below Eq. (16).",
     "13 unit tests pass, among them: the cohort is an integer within its bounds for any rho, the original formula exceeds Cmax for negative rho, and the loss-pair guards hold. No round was cancelled and no update failed in any reproduced run.",
     "The rule returns a valid integer cohort in every round, and the effect of the rounding convention is bounded by one client."),
    ("Replacement 7. R2-09 and R1-18: dynamic range of the cohort and the participation counts",
     "The claim of about 15% fewer clients per round is replaced by the measured saving and its bound, 1 - Cmin/Cmax. The ratio of the loss reduction to the reference rate can replace the absolute reduction, which uses the whole range. Per-round cohort sizes are recorded in every run and are released with the code; the bounds of each configuration are stated; uploads per round and cumulative uploads to a target are reported separately.",
     "Section 4.2 (paragraph below Eq. (16)); Section 5.1 (ablation text); Section 5.4, Cohort size and Table Z.",
     "Table Z. With the absolute rule the mean cohort is 9.71 [9.68, 9.75] over 45 runs (2.9% fewer uploads than a fixed cohort of ten; the cohort is at its maximum in 75% of the rounds). With the ratio rule the mean cohort is 9.10, the smallest cohort 5, and the uploads fall by 7.5% relative to the absolute rule (9.0% relative to a fixed cohort); accuracy differs by -0.29 [-0.57, +0.05] (best round) and -0.08 [-0.55, +0.41] (last 10 rounds) points.",
     "The cohort rule reduces uploads without a detectable change of accuracy, its saving is stated with its upper bound, and the relative-pace measure uses the full range."),
    ("Replacement 8. R1-03 and R2-07: the implemented aggregation, negative scores and dataset size",
     "Eq. (18) defines one weight family S = (1 - kappa) n_i / sum n_j + kappa q_i, where q is the normalised positive part of the stability score. """Evidence for Replacements 9 and 10, recomputed from fedfacs_repro/results/*.json. Writes tools/_work/ev910.json."""
import json
import os
import sys

import numpy as np

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(HERE), "fedfacs_repro"))
import analyze as A  # noqa: E402

rows = A.load()
MAIN_SC = ("s1_0.1", "s1_0.5", "s2")
out = {}


def base(method, sc, ds=None):
    return [r for (d, s, m, seed, tag, r) in rows if m == method and s in sc and tag == "" and (ds is None or d == ds)]


def mean_sd(x, f="{:.2f}"):
    x = np.asarray(x, float)
    return f.format(x.mean()) + (" ± " + f.format(x.std(ddof=1)) if len(x) > 1 else "")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- A. resource accounting (R1-08, R2-01)
res = {}
for m in ["random", "powd", "oort", "divfl", "fedfacs"]:
    rs = base(m, MAIN_SC)
    T = np.array([len(r["log"]["val_acc"]) for r in rs])
    B = np.array([r["bytes_per_model"] for r in rs], float)
    down = np.array([r["log"]["down"][-1] for r in rs]) / B / T
    up = np.array([r["log"]["up"][-1] for r in rs]) / B / T
    aux = np.array([r["log"]["aux"][-1] for r in rs]) / T / 1e3
    steps = np.array([r["log"]["steps"][-1] for r in rs], float) / T
    fwd = np.array([r["log"]["fwd"][-1] for r in rs], float) / T / 1e3
    tot = (np.array([r["log"]["down"][-1] + r["log"]["up"][-1] + r["log"]["aux"][-1] for r in rs])) / 1e9
    wall = np.array([np.mean(r["log"]["wall"]) for r in rs])
    res[m] = dict(n=len(rs), down=down.mean(), up=up.mean(), aux_kb=aux.mean(), steps=steps.mean(), fwd_k=fwd.mean(),
                  total_gb=tot.mean(), wall=wall.mean(), cohort=np.mean([np.mean(r["log"]["cohort"]) for r in rs]))
for m in res:
    res[m]["steps_rel"] = res[m]["steps"] / res["random"]["steps"]
    res[m]["total_rel"] = res[m]["total_gb"] / res["random"]["total_gb"]
    res[m]["wall_rel"] = res[m]["wall"] / res["random"]["wall"]
out["resource"] = res

# paired: FedFACS vs FedAvg-style random, cumulative uploads and total bytes to the common target (r2t)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------- B. fairness (R1-09, R2-15), scenario 3
fair = {}
for ds in ("cifar10", "fmnist"):
    for m in ["random", "powd", "greedy", "fairfedcs", "fedfacs"]:
        rs = [r for (d, s, mm, seed, tag, r) in rows if d == ds and s == "s3" and mm == m and tag == ""]
        if not rs:
            continue
        ms_ = [A.run_metrics(r) for r in rs]
        fair[ds + "|" + m] = dict(n=len(rs), jfi=[x["jfi"] for x in ms_], jfi_q=[x["jfi_q"] for x in ms_],
                                  never=[x["never"] for x in ms_], wait=[x["max_wait"] for x in ms_],
                                  pc_mean=[x["pc_mean"] for x in ms_], pc_std=[x["pc_std"] for x in ms_], pc_p10=[x["pc_p10"] for x in ms_],
                                  acc=[x["acc_best"] for x in ms_])
out["fair"] = fair

# selection-frequency distribution of FedFACS vs random (all main settings): quantiles of selection counts per run
dist = {}
for m in ("fedfacs", "random", "powd"):
    rs = base(m, MAIN_SC)
    q = np.array([np.percentile(r["sel_count"], [0, 10, 50, 90, 100]) for r in rs])
    dist[m] = q.mean(0).tolist()
out["seldist"] = dist

# quality example computed, not asserted
q = np.array([10.0, 5.0]); p = q.copy()
out["example_quality"] = dict(raw=A.jain(p), adj=A.jain(p / q))
x = np.r_[np.ones(90), np.zeros(10)]
out["example_90"] = A.jain(x)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- C. classification metrics (macro averages)
cls = {}
dmax = 0.0
for (d, s, m, seed, tag, r) in rows:
    mm = A.run_metrics(r)
    dmax = max(dmax, abs(mm["acc_from_cm"] - mm["macro_recall"])) if d in ("cifar10", "fmnist", "mnist") else dmax
for ds in ("cifar10", "fmnist", "mnist"):
    for m in ("fedfacs", "random"):
        rs = base(m, MAIN_SC, ds)
        ms_ = [A.run_metrics(r) for r in rs]
        cls[ds + "|" + m] = dict(n=len(rs), acc=[x["acc_from_cm"] for x in ms_], rec=[x["macro_recall"] for x in ms_],
                                 prec=[x["macro_prec"] for x in ms_], f1=[x["macro_f1"] for x in ms_])
out["cls"] = cls
out["cls_max_gap_acc_recall"] = dmax

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- D. protocol audit (R1-21, R2-03, R2-08)
tot = dict(runs=0, ff=0, invalid=0, failed=0, clip=0, bounds=0, cohort_eq=0, wait_ok=0, selcnt_ok=0, up_ok=0, rounds_ok=0)
for (d, s, m, seed, tag, r) in rows:
    lg, cfg = r["log"], r["cfg"]
    tot["runs"] += 1
    tot["invalid"] += r.get("invalid_rounds", 0)
    tot["failed"] += r.get("failed_updates", 0)
    tot["clip"] += r.get("clip_hits", 0)
    if m != "fedfacs":
        continue
    tot["ff"] += 1
    N, T = cfg["N"], len(lg["selected"])
    if all(cfg["cmin"] <= len(sel) <= cfg["cmax"] for sel in lg["selected"]):
        tot["bounds"] += 1
    if all(len(sel) == c for sel, c in zip(lg["selected"], lg["cohort"])):
        tot["cohort_eq"] += 1
    cnt = np.zeros(N, int)
    last = np.zeros(N, int)
    mw = np.zeros(N, int)
    for t, sel in enumerate(lg["selected"], 1):
        for i in sel:
            mw[i] = max(mw[i], t - last[i] - 1)
            last[i] = t
            cnt[i] += 1
    if np.array_equal(cnt, np.array(r["sel_count"])):
        tot["selcnt_ok"] += 1
    if int(mw.max()) == int(max(r["max_wait"])):
        tot["wait_ok"] += 1
    if abs(lg["up"][-1] - sum(lg["cohort"]) * r["bytes_per_model"]) < 1:
        tot["up_ok"] += 1
    if T == cfg["rounds"]:
        tot["rounds_ok"] += 1
out["audit"] = tot

json.dump(out, open(os.path.join(HERE, "_work", "ev910.json"), "w"), indent=1)
print(json.dumps(out["audit"]), out["cls_max_gap_acc_recall"], out["example_quality"], out["example_90"])
for m, v in res.items():
    print(m, {k: round(x, 3) for k, x in v.items()})
print(dist)

"""Evidence for Replacements 9 and 10, recomputed from fedfacs_repro/results/*.json. Writes tools/_work/ev910.json."""
import json
import os
import sys

import numpy as np

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(HERE), "fedfacs_repro"))
import analyze as A  # noqa: E402

rows = A.load()
MAIN_SC = ("s1_0.1", "s1_0.5", "s2")
out = {}


def base(method, sc, ds=None):
    return [r for (d, s, m, seed, tag, r) in rows if m == method and s in sc and tag == "" and (ds is None or d == ds)]


def mean_sd(x, f="{:.2f}"):
    x = np.asarray(x, float)
    return f.format(x.mean()) + (" \u00b1 " + f.format(x.std(ddof=1)) if len(x) > 1 else "")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- A. resource accounting (R1-08, R2-01)
res = {}
for m in ["random", "powd", "oort", "divfl", "fedfacs"]:
    rs = base(m, MAIN_SC)
    T = np.array([len(r["log"]["val_acc"]) for r in rs])
    B = np.array([r["bytes_per_model"] for r in rs], float)
    down = np.array([r["log"]["down"][-1] for r in rs]) / B / T
    up = np.array([r["log"]["up"][-1] for r in rs]) / B / T
    aux = np.array([r["log"]["aux"][-1] for r in rs]) / T / 1e3
    steps = np.array([r["log"]["steps"][-1] for r in rs], float) / T
    fwd = np.array([r["log"]["fwd"][-1] for r in rs], float) / T / 1e3
    tot = (np.array([r["log"]["down"][-1] + r["log"]["up"][-1] + r["log"]["aux"][-1] for r in rs])) / 1e9
    wall = np.array([np.mean(r["log"]["wall"]) for r in rs])
    res[m] = dict(n=len(rs), down=down.mean(), up=up.mean(), aux_kb=aux.mean(), steps=steps.mean(), fwd_k=fwd.mean(),
                  total_gb=tot.mean(), wall=wall.mean(), cohort=np.mean([np.mean(r["log"]["cohort"]) for r in rs]))
for m in res:
    res[m]["steps_rel"] = res[m]["steps"] / res["random"]["steps"]
    res[m]["total_rel"] = res[m]["total_gb"] / res["random"]["total_gb"]
    res[m]["wall_rel"] = res[m]["wall"] / res["random"]["wall"]
out["resource"] = res

# paired: FedFACS vs FedAvg-style random, cumulative uploads and total bytes to the common target (r2t)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------- B. fairness (R1-09, R2-15), scenario 3
fair = {}
for ds in ("cifar10", "fmnist"):
    for m in ["random", "powd", "greedy", "fairfedcs", "fedfacs"]:
        rs = [r for (d, s, mm, seed, tag, r) in rows if d == ds and s == "s3" and mm == m and tag == ""]
        if not rs:
            continue
        ms_ = [A.run_metrics(r) for r in rs]
        fair[ds + "|" + m] = dict(n=len(rs), jfi=[x["jfi"] for x in ms_], jfi_q=[x["jfi_q"] for x in ms_],
                                  never=[x["never"] for x in ms_], wait=[x["max_wait"] for x in ms_],
                                  pc_mean=[x["pc_mean"] for x in ms_], pc_std=[x["pc_std"] for x in ms_], pc_p10=[x["pc_p10"] for x in ms_],
                                  acc=[x["acc_best"] for x in ms_])
out["fair"] = fair

# selection-frequency distribution of FedFACS vs random (all main settings): quantiles of selection counts per run
dist = {}
for m in ("fedfacs", "random", "powd"):
    rs = base(m, MAIN_SC)
    q = np.array([np.percentile(r["sel_count"], [0, 10, 50, 90, 100]) for r in rs])
    dist[m] = q.mean(0).tolist()
out["seldist"] = dist

# quality example computed, not asserted
q = np.array([10.0, 5.0]); p = q.copy()
out["example_quality"] = dict(raw=A.jain(p), adj=A.jain(p / q))
x = np.r_[np.ones(90), np.zeros(10)]
out["example_90"] = A.jain(x)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- C. classification metrics (macro averages)
cls = {}
dmax = 0.0
for (d, s, m, seed, tag, r) in rows:
    mm = A.run_metrics(r)
    dmax = max(dmax, abs(mm["acc_from_cm"] - mm["macro_recall"])) if d in ("cifar10", "fmnist", "mnist") else dmax
for ds in ("cifar10", "fmnist", "mnist"):
    for m in ("fedfacs", "random"):
        rs = base(m, MAIN_SC, ds)
        ms_ = [A.run_metrics(r) for r in rs]
        cls[ds + "|" + m] = dict(n=len(rs), acc=[x["acc_from_cm"] for x in ms_], rec=[x["macro_recall"] for x in ms_],
                                 prec=[x["macro_prec"] for x in ms_], f1=[x["macro_f1"] for x in ms_])
out["cls"] = cls
out["cls_max_gap_acc_recall"] = dmax

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- D. protocol audit (R1-21, R2-03, R2-08)
tot = dict(runs=0, ff=0, invalid=0, failed=0, clip=0, bounds=0, cohort_eq=0, wait_ok=0, selcnt_ok=0, up_ok=0, rounds_ok=0)
for (d, s, m, seed, tag, r) in rows:
    lg, cfg = r["log"], r["cfg"]
    tot["runs"] += 1
    tot["invalid"] += r.get("invalid_rounds", 0)
    tot["failed"] += r.get("failed_updates", 0)
    tot["clip"] += r.get("clip_hits", 0)
    if m != "fedfacs":
        continue
    tot["ff"] += 1
    N, T = cfg["N"], len(lg["selected"])
    if all(cfg["cmin"] <= len(sel) <= cfg["cmax"] for sel in lg["selected"]):
        tot["bounds"] += 1
    if all(len(sel) == c for sel, c in zip(lg["selected"], lg["cohort"])):
        tot["cohort_eq"] += 1
    cnt = np.zeros(N, int)
    last = np.zeros(N, int)
    mw = np.zeros(N, int)
    for t, sel in enumerate(lg["selected"], 1):
        for i in sel:
            mw[i] = max(mw[i], t - last[i] - 1)
            last[i] = t
            cnt[i] += 1
    if np.array_equal(cnt, np.array(r["sel_count"])):
        tot["selcnt_ok"] += 1
    if int(mw.max()) == int(max(r["max_wait"])):
        tot["wait_ok"] += 1
    if abs(lg["up"][-1] - sum(lg["cohort"]) * r["bytes_per_model"]) < 1:
        tot["up_ok"] += 1
    if T == cfg["rounds"]:
        tot["rounds_ok"] += 1
out["audit"] = tot

json.dump(out, open(os.path.join(HERE, "_work", "ev910.json"), "w"), indent=1)
print(json.dumps(out["audit"]), out["cls_max_gap_acc_recall"], out["example_quality"], out["example_90"])
for m, v in res.items():
    print(m, {k: round(x, 3) for k, x in v.items()})
print(dist)

\textbf{Communication and computation cost.} Table~\ref{tab:cost} counts the resources over 100 rounds. FedFACS sends the model to all $N=100$ candidates and trains all of them, so that its downloads and local steps are 10.0 times those of random sampling, while its uploads are 9.71 per round against 10. After 100 rounds the volume of Eq.~(23a) is 5.5 times that of random sampling (368.6 against 67.2~GB). To the common target accuracy FedFACS uploads 520 updates against 555 for random sampling (6.2\% fewer; the target is reached in 44 of 45 runs against 45 of 45), but transmits 198 against 37~GB in total. FedFACS therefore lowers the uploads and not the total communication or the local computation; Power-of-Choice downloads 20 and DivFL 100 models per round for a cohort of ten. The simulated elapsed time per round is 3.4~s against 0.3~s (clients are trained sequentially on one GPU). 

\textbf{Participation fairness.} Table~\ref{tab:fairness} separates three notions. The Jain index of the selection counts (equality of participation) is 0.999 and 0.997 for FedFACS on CIFAR-10 and FMNIST, against 0.919 and 0.919 for random sampling; no client is left unselected and the longest wait is 10 rounds. The quality-adjusted index of Eq.~(24) is lower (0.973 and 0.963) because FedFACS serves the clients almost uniformly and not in proportion to $q_i$: the adjusted index equals one only if $p_i$ is proportional to $q_i$, so that two clients with $q_i=10$ and $q_i=5$ selected twice and once give 1.0 for the adjusted and 0.9 for the raw index. Greedy selection leaves 72\% and 66\% of the clients unselected. The outcome is described by the client-level accuracy: its 10th percentile is 64.0\% and 81.8\% for FedFACS against 64.4\% and 82.4\% for random sampling. 

\textbf{Classification metrics.} Table~\ref{tab:cls} reports the macro-averaged metrics. On CIFAR-10 and FMNIST, whose test sets have equal class sizes, the macro-recall equals the accuracy in every run; on MNIST, whose classes are unbalanced, the two differ by at most 0.92 points. The macro-F1 differs from the macro-recall by at most 0.7 points in every row.
